name: Hierocracy
summary: Hierocracy, or papalism, holds that the pope as Christ's vicar has supreme authority over both spiritual and temporal affairs. Secular rulers hold their office from God and are legitimate, but the spiritual power institutes the temporal and may judge, discipline and in the extreme case depose it, while being judged by no one on earth. Law is developed by canonists through the pope's plenitude of power, and submission to the Roman pontiff is held necessary for salvation.
scope: The medieval papal hierocracy of c. 1075-1325: Gregory VII's Dictatus papae, Boniface VIII's Unam sanctam, and the canonists and theologians Hostiensis, Giles of Rome, James of Viterbo and Augustinus Triumphus. It excludes later Catholic rejection of the deposing power, Protestant and Gallican views, dualists such as John of Paris and Dante, and other clerical regimes (Iranian velayat-e faqih, Byzantine caesaropapism). Most questions on economics, technology and modern identity were never addressed, so those answers are low-confidence inferences or neutral.

keyFigures.name: Pope Gregory VII
keyFigures.role: Pope whose Dictatus papae (1075) set out the claim to depose emperors and judge all.

keyFigures.name: Pope Boniface VIII
keyFigures.role: Issued Unam sanctam (1302), the official statement of the two-swords doctrine.

keyFigures.name: Giles of Rome
keyFigures.role: Author of De ecclesiastica potestate (1302), the fullest theoretical defence of papal fullness of power.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage policy lies outside the hierocratic texts; just-price and just-wage ideas existed but were not part of the papal supremacy doctrine.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Giles of Rome subordinated property to the church's superior right, and usury was a ground for papal intervention, implying distrust of unregulated markets.

unions-good.rationale: Trade unions did not exist; guilds were tolerated but the doctrine concerns church and prince, so no position can be derived.

property-fundamental.rationale: Giles argued the church holds superior direct dominion over all property and can recover goods misused, so property is not fundamental against church authority.

strong-leader.rationale: The papal monarchy of Dictatus Papae favours concentrated authority in one head, but the statement concerns a secular leader bypassing gridlock, which hierocrats would subject to the pope.

state-harmful.rationale: Unam Sanctam says the temporal sword is a real power wielded for the church; temporal authority is necessary and ordained by God, never harmful in itself.

decide-locally.rationale: Dictatus Papae centralizes appeals, legates, councils and appointments in Rome, favouring universal jurisdiction over local autonomy.

traditional-family.rationale: Canonists governed marriage as a sacrament and church jurisdiction, so the church backed the family as a foundation, though this is not the core of hierocracy.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Canon law, the legal tool of hierocracy, treated marriage as a sacrament between man and woman; an adherent would strongly oppose it.

abortion-legal.rationale: Church moral teaching enforced through canon law forbade abortion; hierocrats claim authority over such moral law, so strongly disagree.

more-religion-public.rationale: Unam Sanctam makes spiritual authority superior to temporal power and subjection to the pope necessary for salvation, so public life should be ordered by religion.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Modern question absent from medieval sources; no hierocratic position can be derived.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Hierocrats thought in terms of one universal Christian community under the pope, not national cultures, so the answer is split.

gradual-change.rationale: Dictatus Papae stresses that the Roman church never erred and its rulings stand unless the pope revokes them, favouring established order, but reform (Gregorian) was radical.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The papacy claimed a universal jurisdiction over Christendom, which resembles supranational authority, but UN-style bodies are modern and secular.

nation-first.rationale: Dictatus Papae holds that only the pope may be called universal and that princes answer to him; a single Christian commonwealth outranks national interest.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Just-war and crusade ideas existed under papal authority, but human-rights intervention is modern; split.

revolution-justified.rationale: Hierocrats allowed the pope to depose heretical or tyrannical princes, but lay revolution from below was not licensed; resistance was legitimate only through papal authority.

experts-over-public.rationale: Authority belongs to the clerical hierarchy and canonists, which resembles rule by trained experts, though they are clergy not policy experts.

socialized-markets.rationale: Giles gives the church superior dominion over property but nothing on worker or public enterprise, so this stays neutral.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Central banks did not exist; the doctrine's only monetary concern is the usury ban, which does not settle this.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a monarch who rules, and the statement now asks only about a ceremonial head of state, on which the sources cited here are silent.

reviewHistory.rationale: Hierocrats held that princes' offices were ordained by God and legitimate, though subject to papal judgment; the pope himself is an elective monarch.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a monarch who rules, and the statement now asks only about a ceremonial head of state, on which the sources cited here are silent.

natural-rulers.rationale: Giles argued that spiritual power precedes and outranks the temporal and that priests institute kings, treating clerical rulers as fitted to judge.

political-violence-never.rationale: Unam Sanctam says the temporal sword is wielded for the church at the priest's will, affirming coercive force under religious authority.

separate-church-state.rationale: Unam Sanctam declares that one sword must be subordinated to the other and the temporal subjected to the spiritual, rejecting strict separation.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Hierocracy was elaborated by canonists with the plenitude of power, so law rests on canon law and scriptural claims rather than scripture alone.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The temporal sword is held by the church and used at its bidding, so justice and arms belong to authority under the hierarchy, not firms.

class-struggle-history.rationale: History is ordered by divinely instituted authority and salvation under the church, not class conflict; Marxian claim is foreign to the doctrine.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Reparations for colonialism is a modern claim; the sources give no basis for a view.

civilizational-union.rationale: The hierocratic ideal is one Christian community subject to the Roman pontiff, uniting nations under shared faith.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Giles made lordship depend on justice and fealty to God, not self-interest; selfishness is sin.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Subjection of every creature to the pontiff is described as necessary for salvation, putting obedience to a spiritual order before individual claims.

restore-past-order.rationale: Gregorian reformers presented their claims as restoring the ancient order of the church, but they also innovated; a defensible split.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Policy is judged by conformity to the church's spiritual law and salvation, not results alone.

direct-action.rationale: Action against rulers goes through papal sentences such as excommunication and deposition, not direct popular action.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Giles distinguishes priests, kings and subjects with different offices, so a differentiated social order is basic.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Almsgiving is a church duty but distribution by need as an economic principle is absent from the doctrine.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Power belongs to the spiritual hierarchy, so class dictatorship is rejected.

harm-principle.rationale: The spiritual power judges the temporal for sin and moral failure, so state restriction extends beyond preventing harm.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The doctrine locates rights in an order of offices under the pope and the church, not in individuals.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Dictatus Papae says whoever is not at peace with the Roman church is not Catholic, so exit is not valued.

positive-liberty.rationale: Liberty in the modern sense is not a hierocratic category; the doctrine concerns obedience and salvation.

media-academia-power.rationale: Universities existed in the period but the hierocrats made no claim about their power over rulers.

total-state.rationale: Hierocrats held the pope should not ordinarily exercise temporal power directly and that princes handle temporal affairs, so not a total state.

national-rebirth.rationale: Hierocracy concerns a universal church and not national decadence and rebirth.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Crusading was papal but the doctrine addresses jurisdiction, not expansion.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Dictatus Papae lets the pope release subjects from oaths of fealty to wicked rulers, accepting feudal oaths but placing them under papal judgment.

universal-morality.rationale: The doctrine rests on universal spiritual and moral law judged by the Roman pontiff for all humans.

single-common-good.rationale: A single end, salvation, is guided by the church for all, with temporal government subordinate to it.

national-self-determination.rationale: The pope claims universal authority over princes, so each nation's self-rule is conditional.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Subjection to the pontiff is a matter of faith necessary for salvation, so faith rather than reason alone guides.

ban-interest.rationale: Usury is among the grounds Giles lists for papal intervention in temporal matters, supporting legal prohibition.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The temporal power is instituted by God and the spiritual power, not an instrument of a class.

national-mission.rationale: Hierocrats claim a mission for the church, not a country.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Giles said corrupt princes may be judged, but not a generic claim.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Accountability for state killings is modern; hierocrats held the pope is judged by no one, but this concerns rulers' forces generally.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The church supervises temporal power and spiritual ends, which exceeds a minimal state.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: All human creatures are subject to the pontiff, implying shared status as souls, but offices are ranked.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Canonists maintained separate ecclesiastical jurisdiction over clergy and marriage; a uniform lay code is opposed.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Giles derives rule from church institution and fealty to God, not the governed.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The temporal sword may be used at the church's command, so initiating force is permissible when authorised.

separated-powers.rationale: Giles' fullness of power places spiritual and temporal in one source, rejecting checks between co-equal bodies.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Giles allowed the pope to act outside ordinary law for any cause he deems sufficient, which is a model of emergency prerogative.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: The just-price tradition existed, but papal supremacy texts do not discuss grain price caps.

party-controls-media.rationale: Media were not a concern; the church controlled books but through ecclesiastical, not party, authority.

party-commands-army.rationale: The temporal sword is wielded at the priest's bidding; party command of an army has no place in the doctrine.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The pope claimed supranational authority but EU is secular.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Heads of state command forces but under the pope's direction.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Dictatus Papae places the church under pope, legates and bishops, deposable by the pope, not congregations or assemblies.

clerical-rule.rationale: Unam Sanctam says the spiritual power must institute and judge the earthly power, with the pope as supreme.

recall-officials.rationale: The pope may depose bishops and absolve subjects of fealty, a recall by a higher authority, not voters.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Military alliances and bases are modern topics.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The clergy were the educated class, so hierocrats would not hold this; but there is no documented view.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Citizenship rules did not exist in the form asked, and the doctrine defines membership by baptism and not descent.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Heads of state are not chosen by popular vote under hierocracy; popes are elected by cardinals, and princes inherit.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Giles made dominion conditional on justice and church oversight, so property is justified in service of a higher good and can be recovered when misused.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental risk regulation is modern and unrelated to the supremacy claims of the papalist canonists.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: The sources discuss papal judgment of princes, not the legality of annexations by consent of peoples.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Unam Sanctam asserts the opposite: the temporal power is subjected to the spiritual and judged by it.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Parties were absent; the pope stands above princes but is not nonpartisan symbol.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Hierocrats said princes' office was ordained by God but they were subject to the pope; divine descent of rulers is not claimed.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Giles held the pope is bound by no earthly law and may act outside ordinary law, though bound by divine law, so the supreme ruler is unbound by positive law.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The pope holds the fullness of power and the church is an internal monarchy; a mixed constitution is not the model.

leader-cult.rationale: Dictatus Papae claims his is the only name spoken in churches, which sits near honours for one leader, but the statement concerns a national leader.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist question with no hierocratic content.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Giles lists heresy as ground for papal intervention and unbelievers are not true owners, supporting legal penalties for leaving the faith.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Minority cultural institutions are a modern nationalities question absent from the doctrine.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: History is seen through providential spiritual order.

ban-cartels.rationale: Competition law is modern; the nearest medieval concern is just price and usury, which is not about cartels.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Hierocrats accepted hereditary princes and nobles while subjecting them to papal judgment.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Giles denied that unbelievers hold true lordship, which licenses rule over them by the faithful.

patriotic-education.rationale: Hierocrats favour loyalty to the church rather than to a nation, so this is split.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Modern American debate with no hierocratic content.

public-money-creation.rationale: Money creation by banks or a public body is a modern question; only usury is addressed by the doctrine.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: A debate within Marxism and economics, not touched by the medieval papalists.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Giles' view that the pope is bound by no human law and judged by God alone conflicts with entrenched human limits.

elective-rulers.rationale: The pope is elected, but hierocrats accepted hereditary princes; Innocent IV allowed papal choice of a monarch when a throne is vacant.

minority-veto.rationale: Dictatus Papae says the pope alone makes laws and judges all, binding dissenters.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The papal deposing power allowed removal of rulers for heresy or extreme misgovernment, though through the pope not by subjects acting alone.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Supreme lawmaking authority sits with the pope.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Mass media did not exist; the claim comes from modern critical theory, not hierocracy.

native-born-offices.rationale: The sources discuss papal control of church offices, not birth requirements for state posts.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Giles denies unbelievers true lordship, which cuts against such claims for non-Christians, but the question is modern.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: A question of American history with no connection to medieval papalism.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Canonists administered marriage law and treated marriage as indissoluble, so ending a marriage at will conflicts with that law.

recallable-delegates.rationale: The pope can depose bishops but only from above; recall by those below is not the model.

single-official-language.rationale: Latin as church language, but not a state-language doctrine.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Foreign funding of NGOs and universities is a modern issue not found in the sources.

job-guarantee.rationale: State employment of last resort is modern, so the papalist texts give no basis for a view.

democratic-peace.rationale: A modern international-relations claim; hierocrats did not consider democracies.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Subjection is necessary for salvation; Dictatus Papae calls for obedience, so a general duty to obey rightful authority exists.

non-intervention.rationale: The pope may judge and depose foreign princes, rejecting non-interference.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Marriage was a sacrament governed by canon law.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Dictatus Papae makes the pope the judge of princes and universal, so higher law outranks national constitutions.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Dictatus Papae says all princes must kiss the pope's feet, a ritual deference to the leading authority.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Public-service delivery models are modern, so the doctrine gives no guidance.

religion-illusion.rationale: Unam Sanctam makes the church and subjection to the pontiff necessary for salvation, treating religion as true.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: A Marxist historical judgment with no hierocratic counterpart.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Language purism is a modern nationalist concern, not found in the sources.

majority-settlement.rationale: Settlement policies in minority regions are modern and absent from the doctrine.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: A twentieth-century third-way slogan with no hierocratic counterpart.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Papal claim to lands via the Donation of Constantine.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Heresy named as ground for papal intervention supports suppression of religious dissent.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Giles names sacrilege and heresy as grounds for papal intervention in temporal matters, so civil punishment of false worship is endorsed.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: An Islamic concept; the closest hierocratic analogue is crusading under papal call, which is not the same claim.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The pope could declare a heretical ruler deposed and release subjects from allegiance, although by papal sentence not by private force.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Dictatus Papae gives all power of appointment to the pope; broad participation is not the model.

assisted-dying.rationale: Canon law enforced church moral doctrine that life is God's gift, so assisted killing would be opposed.

alienated-labor.rationale: A Marxist concept foreign to the papalist texts.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Giles denies unbelievers true lordship, but the question of Islam and Western values is modern.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Unam Sanctam says all power is ordained by God and flows through the spiritual power that institutes the earthly.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Unam Sanctam affirms the temporal sword as a real power wielded for the church, so abolition is rejected.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Hierocrats accepted hereditary princes while claiming judgment over them.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Usury prohibition is stated but mutual banks are not.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Printing did not exist and the claim comes from modern radical thought.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Giles' pope is a creature without halter or bridle who may act outside ordinary law.

open-government-data.rationale: Open records are modern; the sources describe a papal power acting at its own discretion.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Dictatus Papae says the Roman church has never erred and never will, resisting reinterpretation by others.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The papalist texts do not link wealth concentration to liberty.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Unam Sanctam makes subjection to the pontiff necessary for salvation, opposing state atheism.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Church charity was central, but hierocrats also expect princes to act under church guidance, so this is split.

vote-delegation.rationale: Liquid democracy is modern and unconnected to the doctrine.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Extinction risk is a modern concern not found in the medieval texts.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: The clerical hierarchy of the pope, legates and bishops was male only.

abolish-ip.rationale: Patents and copyright are modern, so there is no hierocratic position.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Nuclear basing is modern and unrelated to medieval papalism.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Unam Sanctam affirms the temporal sword; just force is lawful, so a ban on killing in defence is rejected.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The temporal order is judged by the spiritual power and is directed to salvation.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Ethnic economic nationalism is modern and absent from the sources.

second-chamber.rationale: Bicameral legislatures are modern; the papalists described no legislature.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Dictatus Papae centralizes appeals, councils and appointments in Rome, opposing confederation of free towns.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Drug regulation is modern and unrelated to the doctrine.

person-over-state.rationale: Hierocrats value persons as souls, but also hold the temporal power must serve spiritual ends; split.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The doctrine rests on the claim that humans have a spiritual end served by the church, with temporal government subordinate.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Dictatus Papae shows central authority revoking and transferring local offices.

communal-electorates.rationale: Separate religious electorates are modern; the papalist texts propose no electoral scheme.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: A modern nationalist claim not found in the sources.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Pollution pricing is modern and unrelated to the doctrine.

arms-reduction.rationale: Arms limitation is modern; the sources only affirm the temporal sword.

capital-controls.rationale: Cross-border capital flows are modern, so there is no hierocratic view.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Legal borrowing limits are modern and unrelated to the doctrine.

sacred-nation.rationale: Hierocrats hold the church, not the nation, as sacred community.

internal-colonialism.rationale: A modern theory of regional exploitation absent from the texts.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Every human creature is declared subject to the Roman pontiff, assuming a common nature and end.

public-service-media.rationale: Public broadcasting is modern and unrelated to the doctrine.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Unam Sanctam declares that submission to the Roman pontiff is necessary for salvation and that there is one holy Catholic church outside which there is no salvation.

one-language-many-names.rationale: The papal hierocracy was universal and Latin-based; the question of vernacular naming was outside it.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: The doctrine places lawmaking in the pope's plenitude of power, while accepting that temporal rulers act under custom; no stated view on advisory chiefs.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Unam Sanctam holds that submission to the Roman pontiff is necessary for salvation, so no rival interpretation could stand level with the pope's in law.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: The spiritual power institutes and may depose the temporal ruler, so legitimacy comes from the pope and God, not from electoral choice and removal of rulers.

simple-living.rationale: Voluntary poverty was praised in monastic ideals but the doctrine is about papal jurisdiction, not lifestyle; no view is stated.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Medieval papal writers said nothing about a national spiritual bond to land; this is an inference that the question was simply outside their frame.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Parties did not exist; the hierocrats built a hierarchy through the pope rather than popular mediation, but the statement does not fit the period, so neutral.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Unam Sanctam holds that there is one church outside which there is no salvation, and the Dictatus Papae makes the Roman church the sole standard, so a politics organised among rival denominations is rejected.

national-resource-control.rationale: Resource control was not a hierocratic question; the pope claimed supreme universal authority above national boundaries.

multipolar-world.rationale: Unam Sanctam asserts one supreme authority over all, so independent centres of power equal in standing are rejected.

missingStatements.text: The pope should have the power to depose a ruler and release that ruler's subjects from their allegiance.
missingStatements.rationale: Dictatus papae claims that the pope may depose emperors and release subjects from fealty to wicked rulers, and the deposing power was later exercised against Henry IV.

missingStatements.text: The highest religious authority should be able to judge the rulers of states, and no earthly authority may judge it in return.
missingStatements.rationale: Unam sanctam says the spiritual power judges the temporal while the highest power can be judged by God alone, and Dictatus papae says no one may judge the pope.

missingStatements.text: Religious authority holds the superior right over all property, and laypeople hold it only by use and on condition of just conduct.
missingStatements.rationale: Giles of Rome argued the church has direct dominion over all property and can recover goods misused, a distinctive hierocratic claim no statement captures.
missingStatements.declined: Giles of Rome's dominion thesis is idiosyncratic to medieval canon-law writers; property-serves-common-good covers the modern contested question.

notes: Hierocracy is strongest on church-state, authority and law statements; most economic and modern-identity statements are neutral or low-confidence inferences because the doctrine was a medieval jurisdictional theory. Dualists like John of Paris and Dante, and later Catholic theologians such as Bellarmine and Suarez, rejected the full claim.
